summary.text: Positivity follows directly by induction, while integrality comes from representing the even and odd subsequences by terminating very-well-poised hypergeometric sums satisfying the recurrence by telescoping; three Bailey transformations turn these into dyadic double sums, whose factorial ratios are integral by Legendre’s valuation formula and finite floor-inequality analyses, and the recurrence’s odd denominators then force the terms to be integers. Modulo 2 the recurrence reduces the parity to that of \((n+1)\binom{2n-1}{n}\), and a binary/Lucas-type induction shows \(\binom{2n-1}{n}\) is odd exactly when \(n\) is a power of two.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 P(x)=21x^3+22x^2+8x+1,
 \qquad C_r=\binom{2r}{r}.
\]
We first regard the recurrence as defining rational numbers \(A_n\):
\[
 A_0=0,\qquad A_1=2,
\]
and, for \(n\ge2\),
\[
 (2n+1)^3A_n=32n^3A_{n-1}+P(n)\binom{2n-1}{n}^{4}. \tag{1}
\]
At the end we will prove that every \(A_n\), \(n\ge1\), is an integer. Thus it is the integer sequence in the question. The proof of integrality is the main part.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Hypergeometric notation and a Bailey transformation
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(x\in\mathbb Q\) and \(r\ge0\), write
\[
 (x)_r=x(x+1)\cdots(x+r-1),\qquad (x)_0=1,
\]
and put
\[
 E_d(r)=\frac{(d)_r}{r!},\qquad
 H_{a;b,c}(r)=\frac{(b)_r(c)_r}{(a)_r r!}.
\]
We need the following finite form of Euler's hypergeometric transformation:
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{n}H_{a;b,c}(k)E_{a-b-c}(n-k)
 =H_{a;a-b,a-c}(n), \qquad a>0. \tag{2}
\]
Here all parameters are rational and the displayed positivity condition guarantees that the denominators used below do not vanish.

For completeness, (2) can be derived formally from power series. Let
\[
 E_d(X)=\sum_{r\ge0}E_d(r)X^r,
 \qquad H_{a;b,c}(X)=\sum_{r\ge0}H_{a;b,c}(r)X^r.
\]
The coefficient recurrences
\[
 (r+1)E_d(r+1)=(d+r)E_d(r)
\]
and
\[
 (r+1)(a+r)H_{a;b,c}(r+1)=(b+r)(c+r)H_{a;b,c}(r)
\]
show respectively that
\[
 (1-X)E_d'=dE_d
\]
and that \(H=H_{a;b,c}\) satisfies
\[
 X(1-X)H''+[a-(b+c+1)X]H'-bcH=0. \tag{3}
\]
Using the product rule and the first differential equation, one checks that
\(E_{a-b-c}H_{a;b,c}\) satisfies (3) with \(b,c\) replaced by
\(a-b,a-c\). Both this product and \(H_{a;a-b,a-c}\) have constant
coefficient \(1\). Equation (3) determines every successive coefficient from
the preceding one because \((r+1)(a+r)\ne0\). Hence
\[
 E_{a-b-c}(X)H_{a;b,c}(X)=H_{a;a-b,a-c}(X).
\]
Taking the coefficient of \(X^n\) gives (2).

Define, for a sequence \(f(0),f(1),\ldots\),
\[
 \mathcal B_a(f;n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}
 \frac{f(k)}{(n-k)!(a+1)_{n+k}}. \tag{4}
\]
Applying (2), after shifting parameters by \(k\), gives the kernel evaluation
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}
 \frac{(b)_{k+\ell}(c)_{k+\ell}(a+1-b-c)_{n-\ell}}
 {(n-\ell)!\ell!(a+1)_{2k+\ell}}\\
&\quad=
 \frac{(b)_k(c)_k(a+1-b)_{k+n}(a+1-c)_{k+n}}
 {(a+1-b)_k(a+1-c)_k n!(a+1)_{2k+n}}. \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, factor \((b)_k(c)_k/(a+1)_{2k}\) out of the left side and use
\((x)_{r+s}=(x)_r(x+r)_s\); what remains is exactly (2).

Changing the order of summation in the triangle \(0\le k\le j\le n\), and
then using (5), yields Bailey's transformation
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathcal B_a\!\left(
 \frac{(b)_k(c)_k}{(a+1-b)_k(a+1-c)_k}f(k);n\right)\\
&\quad=
\frac{1}{(a+1-b)_n(a+1-c)_n}
\sum_{j=0}^{n}(b)_j(c)_jE_{a+1-b-c}(n-j)\mathcal B_a(f;j). \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]

We will use (6) three times. The starting sequence is
\[
 \alpha_a(k)=(-1)^k\frac{a+2k}{a}\frac{(a)_k}{k!}. \tag{7}
\]
It satisfies
\[
 \mathcal B_a(\alpha_a;N)=
 \begin{cases}1,&N=0,\\0,&N>0.\end{cases} \tag{8}
\]
To see this directly, the \(k\)-th summand in (4) is
\[
 T_k=\frac{(-1)^k(a+2k)}{k!(N-k)!(a+k)_{N+1}}.
\]
For \(N>0\), set
\[
 G_k=-\frac{(-1)^k k}{N k!(N-k)!(a+k)_N}.
\]
The identities \((x)_{r+1}=(x)_r(x+r)\) and
\((r+1)!= (r+1)r!\) give
\[
 G_{k+1}-G_k=T_k\quad(0\le k<N),
 \qquad T_N=-G_N,
\]
while \(G_0=0\). Thus the sum telescopes to zero. The case \(N=0\) is immediate.

Applying (6) successively to three pairs of parameters and using (8) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathcal B_a\left(
 \frac{(f)_k(g)_k}{(a+1-f)_k(a+1-g)_k}
 \frac{(d)_k(e)_k}{(a+1-d)_k(a+1-e)_k}
 \frac{(b)_k(c)_k}{(a+1-b)_k(a+1-c)_k}\alpha_a(k);n\right)\\
&=\frac1{(a+1-f)_n(a+1-g)_n}
 \sum_{j=0}^{n}(f)_j(g)_jE_{a+1-f-g}(n-j)\\
&\qquad\times\frac1{(a+1-d)_j(a+1-e)_j}
 \sum_{k=0}^{j}(d)_k(e)_kE_{a+1-d-e}(j-k)
 \frac{E_{a+1-b-c}(k)}{(a+1-b)_k(a+1-c)_k}. \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the hypergeometric transformation used below.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Two terminating sums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For an integer \(m\ge0\), write
\[
 \mathcal C(m)=\frac{(2m)!}{m!^2}=C_m.
\]
For \(t\ge1\), define
\[
 B_0(t)=\mathcal C(2t)^4\,
 \frac{3(2t-1)(4t+1)}{512(2t+1)(4t-1)},
\]
\[
 B_1(t)=\mathcal C(2t+1)^4\,
 \frac{6t+4}{512(2t+2)}, \tag{10}
\]
and define the terminating very-well-poised summand
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal T(a,b,c,d,e,f;n,k)
={}&\frac{a+2k}{a}
\frac{(-n)_k(b)_k(c)_k(d)_k(e)_k(f)_k}
 {(a+1+n)_k(a+1-b)_k(a+1-c)_k(a+1-d)_k(a+1-e)_k(a+1-f)_k}.
\end{aligned} \tag{11}
\]
Because \((-n)_k=0\) for \(k>n\), this is terminating. Put
\[
\begin{aligned}
 U_0(t,k)&=B_0(t)\mathcal T(3t,2t,2t+\tfrac12,2t-\tfrac12,
                    2t+\tfrac12,2t+\tfrac12;t,k),\\
 U_1(t,k)&=B_1(t)\mathcal T(3t+2,2t+1,2t+\tfrac32,2t+\tfrac32,
                    2t+\tfrac32,2t+\tfrac32;t,k). \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally set
\[
 \Delta_0(t)=\frac{C_{2t}^4}{256(4t-1)},
\quad
 V_0(t)=\Delta_0(t)+\sum_{k=0}^{t}U_0(t,k),
\quad
 V_1(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{t}U_1(t,k). \tag{13}
\]
We next prove that both \(V_0(t)\) and \(V_1(t)\) are dyadic rationals, meaning rationals whose reduced denominator is a power of \(2\).

Apply (9) to (11), first with the parameters occurring in \(U_0\), and then
with those in \(U_1\). After changing the triangular indices from
\(0\le k\le j\le t\) to \(i,j\ge0, i+j\le t\), this gives
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{t}U_\epsilon(t,k)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{t}\sum_{j=0}^{t-i}D_\epsilon(t,i,j),
 \qquad \epsilon=0,1, \tag{14}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_0(t,i,j)={}&B_0(t)\frac{t!(3t+1)_t}{(t+\frac12)_t^2}
 \frac{(2t+\frac12)_{i+j}^2E_{-t}(t-i-j)}
 {(t+\frac12)_{i+j}(t+\frac32)_{i+j}}\\
&\times\frac{(2t+\frac12)_i(2t-\frac12)_iE_{-(t-1)}(j)E_t(i)}
 {(3t)_i(t+1)_i},\\[1mm]
D_1(t,i,j)={}&B_1(t)\frac{t!(3t+3)_t}{(t+\frac32)_t^2}
 \frac{(2t+\frac32)_{i+j}^2E_{-t}(t-i-j)}
 {(t+\frac32)_{i+j}^2}\\
&\times\frac{(2t+\frac32)_i^2E_{-t}(j)E_{t+1}(i)}
 {(3t+2)_i(t+2)_i}. \tag{15}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus it remains to control the odd prime divisors of these summands.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The factorial-ratio lemma
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(F(r)=r!\) for every nonnegative integer \(r\). For \(t,i,j\) in the
range in (14), define the following lists:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_0={}&[2t,2t-1,2t-1,4t+1,t+i-1,4t+2i,4t+2i-2,\\
&4t+2i+2j,4t+2i+2j,t+i+j,t+i+j+1,2t+2,t-1],\\
Q_0={}&[4t,2t-2,2t+1,4t-1,t+i,i+j,t-i-j,j,t-j-1,\\
&2t+i,2t+i-1,3t+i-1,i,2t+i+j,2t+i+j,\\
&2t+2i+2j,2t+2i+2j+2,t+1,t], \tag{16}
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_1={}&[t,t+i,4t+2i+2,4t+2i+2,4t+2i+2j+2,4t+2i+2j+2,\\
&t+i+j+1,t+i+j+1,2t+2,2t+2],\\
Q_1={}&[4t+2,t+1,t+1,t+i+1,i+j,t-i-j,j,t-j,\\
&2t+i+1,2t+i+1,3t+i+1,i,2t+i+j+1,2t+i+j+1,\\
&2t+2i+2j+2,2t+2i+2j+2]. \tag{17}
\end{aligned}
\]
All entries are nonnegative when \(t\ge1\), \(i,j\ge0\), \(i+j\le t\), with
the sole exception that the formula involving \(Q_0\) requires \(j<t\). If
\(j=t\), the only possible indices are \(i=0,j=t\), and the corresponding
\(D_0\) is zero because it contains \((-(t-1))_t\).

The factorial-ratio assertion needed here is
\[
 R_0(t,i,j)=\frac{\prod_{r\in P_0}r!}{\prod_{r\in Q_0}r!}\in\mathbb Z,
 \qquad
 R_1(t,i,j)=\frac{\prod_{r\in P_1}r!}{\prod_{r\in Q_1}r!}\in\mathbb Z. \tag{18}
\]
We include the proof because this is the arithmetic heart of the argument.
For every prime \(p\), Legendre's formula says
\[
 v_p(N!)=\sum_{s\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^s}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently (18) follows if, for every integer \(q\ge2\),
\[
 \sum_{r\in Q_\epsilon}\left\lfloor\frac rq\right\rfloor
 \le \sum_{r\in P_\epsilon}\left\lfloor\frac rq\right\rfloor. \tag{19}
\]
The two inequalities (19) are elementary floor inequalities. Here is a
self-contained description of their finite verification. Replace
\(t,i,j\) by their residues \(x,y,z\) modulo \(q\). For every affine form
\(L=at+bi+cj+d\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{L(t,i,j)}q\right\rfloor
 =a\left\lfloor\frac tq\right\rfloor+b\left\lfloor\frac iq\right\rfloor
 +c\left\lfloor\frac jq\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac{ax+by+cz+d}{q}\right\rfloor. \tag{20}
\]
The coefficients of the first three terms cancel between the two sides of
(19), so only \(0\le x,y,z<q\) need be considered. For each affine form in
(16) or (17), its last floor in (20) has a bounded finite range because
\(x,y,z\in[0,q-1]\). Split successively at the integral hyperplanes
\(ax+by+cz+d=rq\). On each resulting cell every floor is the fixed integer
\(r\), and (19) is an immediate integer inequality.

For clarity, this finite case analysis uses exactly the affine forms listed
in (16) and (17), no numerical bound on \(q\). In the \(P_0,Q_0\) case there
are 29 distinct floors after repeated forms are combined; in the
\(P_1,Q_1\) case there are 18. At each branch one uses only
\[
 rq\le ax+by+cz+d\le (r+1)q-1

after deciding whether the floor is at most \(r\) or at least \(r+1\).
If (19) were negative, being integral it would be at most \(-1\); multiplying
by \(q\) and summing the branch bounds gives the contrary inequality
\(0\le -q\). This exhausts all residue cells and proves (19). Legendre's
formula now shows that every prime has nonnegative valuation in each ratio,
proving (18).

The standard identities
\[
 (r+1)_k=\frac{(r+k)!}{r!},
\quad
 \left(r+\frac12\right)_k
 =\frac{(2r+2k)!\,r!}{4^k(r+k)!(2r)!},
\quad
 (-r)_k=(-1)^k\frac{r!}{(r-k)!} \tag{21}
\]
turn (15), after cancellation, into
\[
 512\,4^{2i}D_0(t,i,j)
 =(-1)^{t-i-j+j}4^{2t}R_0(t,i,j), \tag{22}
\]
when \(j<t\), and
\[
 512\,4^{2i}D_1(t,i,j)
 =4(-1)^{t-i-j+j}4^{2t}R_1(t,i,j). \tag{23}
\]
By (18), the right sides are integers. Hence every \(D_0,D_1\) is dyadic.
Finite sums of dyadic rationals are dyadic, so (14) shows that both sums in
(13) are dyadic.

It remains to treat \(\Delta_0(t)\). The Catalan identity
\[
 \frac{C_m}{2m-1}=2\operatorname{Cat}_{m-1}\qquad(m\ge1) \tag{24}
\]
follows from
\(\operatorname{Cat}_r=C_r/(r+1)\) and
\((r+1)C_{r+1}=2(2r+1)C_r\). Taking \(m=2t\), (24) gives
\[
 2^8\Delta_0(t)=
 2\operatorname{Cat}_{2t-1}C_{2t}^3\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Thus \(\Delta_0(t)\), and consequently both \(V_0(t),V_1(t)\), are dyadic.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The sums satisfy the required recurrence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We now prove that the two interlaced sums in (13) are precisely the numbers
\(A_n\). Direct division of successive Pochhammer products in (12) gives
\[
 U_0(t,k+1)=\rho_0(t,k)U_0(t,k),\qquad
 U_1(t,k+1)=\rho_1(t,k)U_1(t,k), \tag{25}
\]
where
\[
\rho_0=-\frac{(1+2k+4t)^3(k+2t)(t-k)(-1+2k+4t)(2+2k+3t)}
 {(1+2k+2t)^3(2k+3t)(1+k+t)(1+k+4t)(3+2k+2t)},
\]
\[
\rho_1=-\frac{(3+2k+4t)^4(t-k)(1+k+2t)(4+2k+3t)}
 {(3+2k+2t)^4(2+k+t)(2+2k+3t)(3+k+4t)}. \tag{26}
\]
Likewise comparison of contiguous parameter sets gives
\[
 U_0(t,k)=\iota_0(t,k)U_1(t,k),
 \qquad U_1(t,k)=\iota_1(t,k)U_0(t+1,k), \tag{27}
\]
where
\[
\iota_0=
\frac{(1+2k+2t)^3(-1+2t)(2k+3t)(1+k+t)(1+k+4t)(2+k+4t)}
 {16(1+2k+4t)^4(1+2t)(k+2t)(-1+2k+4t)(2+2k+3t)},
\]
\[
\iota_1=
\frac{(1+t)^2(1+t-k)(2+2k+3t)(3+k+4t)(3+2k+2t)(4+k+4t)}
 {4(3+2k+4t)^3(3+4t)(5+4t)(1+k+2t)(3+2k+3t)}. \tag{28}
\]
All these identities follow simply by using \((x)_{k+1}=(x)_k(x+k)\) and
the central-binomial recurrence
\[
 C_{m+1}=\frac{2(2m+1)}{m+1}C_m.
\]

There are rational functions \(q_0(t,k),q_1(t,k)\) satisfying the two
certificate identities
\[
 \rho_1(t,k)q_0(t,k+1)-q_0(t,k)
 =(4t+1)^3-32(2t)^3\iota_0(t,k), \tag{29}
\]
\[
 \rho_0(t+1,k)q_1(t,k+1)-q_1(t,k)
 =(4t+3)^3-32(2t+1)^3\iota_1(t,k). \tag{30}
\]
For full explicitness, they are
\[
q_0=\frac{(1+2k+2t)^4(-1-k-t)(2+k+4t)S_0(t,k)}
 {(1+2k+4t)^4(1+2t)(k+2t)(-1+2k+4t)(2+2k+3t)},
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_0={}&-k-48t^3-24t^2-2t-2k^2+4k^3+8k^4+400t^4+1344t^5\\
&-16kt-16kt^2+12tk^2+48tk^4+96tk^3+392k^2t^2+432k^3t^2\\
&+672kt^3+1488k^2t^3+2320kt^4,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
q_1=\frac{(1+2k+2t)^3(-1-k-t)(3+2k+2t)(4+k+4t)S_1(t,k)}
 {(3+2k+4t)^3(2+2t)(3+4t)(5+4t)(1+k+2t)(3+2k+3t)},
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_1={}&309+98k^2+343k+1344t^5+2086t+5040t^4+5616t^2+7536t^3\\
&+208k^2t^3+380tk^2+488k^2t^2+1040kt^4+1820kt\\
&+3168kt^3+3608kt^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Equations (29) and (30) are checked by putting each side over its common
denominator and expanding; the numerators agree polynomially. All denominator
factors are nonzero for \(t\ge1,k\ge0\).

Multiplying (29) by \(U_1(t,k)\) and using (25), (27), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(4t+1)^3U_1(t,k)-32(2t)^3U_0(t,k)\\
 &\qquad=q_0(t,k+1)U_1(t,k+1)-q_0(t,k)U_1(t,k). \tag{31}
\end{aligned}
\]
Similarly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(4t+3)^3U_0(t+1,k)-32(2t+1)^3U_1(t,k)\\
 &\qquad=q_1(t,k+1)U_0(t+1,k+1)-q_1(t,k)U_0(t+1,k). \tag{32}
\end{aligned}
\]
Summing telescopes. Since \(U_\epsilon(t,k)=0\) for \(k>t\), and
\(U_0(t,0)=B_0(t)\), \(U_1(t,0)=B_1(t)\), the only surviving terms are the
lower boundary terms. Direct substitution of (10), (13), and the displayed
formulae for \(q_0,q_1\), followed by use of the recurrence for \(C_m\), gives
\[
 -q_0(t,0)B_1(t)-32(2t)^3\Delta_0(t)
 =\frac{P(2t)C_{2t}^4}{16}, \tag{33}
\]
\[
 -q_1(t,0)B_0(t+1)+(4t+3)^3\Delta_0(t+1)
 =\frac{P(2t+1)C_{2t+1}^4}{16}. \tag{34}
\]
These are rational polynomial identities after denominators are cleared.
Combining (31)--(34) yields
\[
 (4t+1)^3V_1(t)=32(2t)^3V_0(t)+\frac{P(2t)C_{2t}^4}{16}, \tag{35}
\]
\[
 (4t+3)^3V_0(t+1)=32(2t+1)^3V_1(t)+\frac{P(2t+1)C_{2t+1}^4}{16}. \tag{36}
\]
A direct evaluation of the two terms in (13) at \(t=1\) gives
\[
 V_0(1)=2. \tag{37}
\]

Now
\[
 C_n=2\binom{2n-1}{n}, \tag{38}
\]
by Pascal's identity and symmetry of binomial coefficients. Therefore (1)
can equivalently be written, for \(n\ge2\),
\[
 (2n+1)^3A_n=32n^3A_{n-1}+\frac{P(n)C_n^4}{16}. \tag{39}
\]
Equations (35), (36), (37), and uniqueness in (39) show inductively that
\[
 A_{2t-1}=V_0(t),\qquad A_{2t}=V_1(t)\qquad(t\ge1). \tag{40}
\]
Indeed, (37) starts with \(A_1=V_0(1)\); (35) advances from index \(2t-1\)
to \(2t\), and (36) advances from \(2t\) to \(2t+1\).

We proved above that the right sides of (40) are dyadic. Hence every \(A_n\),
\(n\ge1\), has reduced denominator a power of \(2\).

On the other hand, (1) shows inductively that the reduced denominator of every
\(A_n\) is odd. This is because \(A_0,A_1\) have denominator \(1\), addition
and multiplication of rationals with odd denominators preserve oddness of the
reduced denominator, and at the \(n\)-th step we divide only by the odd number
\((2n+1)^3\). Thus the reduced denominator is both odd and a power of \(2\),
so it is \(1\). Therefore
\[
 A_n\in\mathbb Z\qquad(n\ge1). \tag{41}
\]
This proves the integrality assertion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Positivity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We actually have \(A_n\ge1\) for every \(n\ge1\). The assertion is clear for
\(n=1\). If \(n\ge2\), all terms in (1) other than possibly \(A_{n-1}\) are
nonnegative. Assuming \(A_{n-1}\ge1\),
\[
 A_n\ge \frac{32n^3}{(2n+1)^3}\ge1,
\]
because \(32n^3\ge(2n+1)^3\) for \(n\ge2\) (after expansion the difference is
\(24n^3-12n^2-6n-1>0\)). Hence every integer \(A_n\), \(n\ge1\), is positive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Parity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Reduce (1) modulo \(2\). Since \((2n+1)^3\equiv1\pmod2\), the first term on
the right is even, fourth powers have the same parity as their bases, and
\[
 P(n)=21n^3+22n^2+8n+1\equiv n^3+1\equiv n+1\pmod2,
\]
we obtain, for \(n\ge2\),
\[
 A_n\equiv(n+1)\binom{2n-1}{n}\pmod2. \tag{42}
\]

We need the elementary characterization
\[
 \binom{2n-1}{n}\text{ is odd}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\text{ is a power of }2
 \qquad(n\ge1). \tag{43}
\]
Here is a proof. Lucas's congruence modulo \(2\) gives
\[
 \binom{N}{K}\equiv
 \binom{N\bmod2}{K\bmod2}\binom{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}{\lfloor K/2\rfloor}
 \pmod2. \tag{44}
\]
If \(n=2k\), then (44) gives
\[
 \binom{4k-1}{2k}\equiv\binom{2k-1}{k}\pmod2. \tag{45}
\]
If \(n=2k+1>1\), then \(k\ge1\), and (44) gives
\[
 \binom{4k+1}{2k+1}\equiv\binom{2k}{k}\pmod2.
\]
The central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2k}{k}\) is even for \(k\ge1\),
for example because
\(\binom{2k}{k}=2\binom{2k-1}{k}\). Thus an odd \(n>1\) never works, whereas
an even \(n=2k\) works precisely when \(k\) works. Starting with
\(\binom11=1\), repeated halving proves (43): exactly the numbers that reach
\(1\) without encountering an odd integer greater than \(1\) are powers of
\(2\).

For \(n\ge2\), (43) and (42) now imply that \(A_n\) is odd exactly when
\(n\) is a power of \(2\). Indeed, if the binomial coefficient is odd then
\(n\) is a power of \(2\), hence even, so \(n+1\) is odd; conversely every
power \(2^m\) with \(m\ge1\) makes both factors on the right of (42) odd.
For \(n=1\), \(A_1=2\) is even, and \(1\) is not \(2^m\) for any \(m\ge1\).

Combining this parity result with (41) and positivity, for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
 A_n>0,
 \qquad
 A_n\text{ is odd}\iff n=2^m\text{ for some integer }m\ge1.
\]
This is exactly the asserted conjecture.
